name: MathlibAnnex.CStarAlgebra.CAR.tendsto_norm_compressionError
title: Root compression becomes scalar in norm

content.assumptions: The stages are linked by $a\mapsto a\otimes I_2$, and $A$ is their norm completion. The functional $\omega$ is the continuous root state. Each $f_n$ is a self-adjoint projection of norm at most one. The element $x$ is arbitrary but fixed while $n$ tends to infinity.
content.conclusion: Writing $E_n(x)=f_nxf_n-\omega(x)f_n$, the theorem gives $\lim_{n\to\infty}\|E_n(x)\|=0$ for every $x\in A$. The error $E_n(x)$ is an element of $A$; its norm is the real-valued quantity that converges.
content.display_title: Root compression becomes scalar in norm
content.lean_realization_notes: This is pointwise convergence in $x$, not convergence in operator norm uniformly over the unit ball. It also does not assert norm convergence of the projections $f_n$. The displayed projections have rank one at their defining finite stage; no rank-one assertion in an arbitrary representation of $A$ is used.
content.natural_language_statement: Let $A$ be the completed CAR algebra with stage maps $\iota_n:M_{2^n}(\mathbb C)\to A$ and root state $\omega(\iota_n(a))=a_{00}$. Put $f_n=\iota_n(E_{00})$, where $E_{00}$ is the projection onto the first coordinate. Then, for every fixed $x\in A$, $\|f_nxf_n-\omega(x)f_n\|\longrightarrow0$ as $n\to\infty$.
content.one_sentence_role: Extends an exact rank-one compression identity on finite stages to a pointwise norm limit on the completed algebra.

proof_steps.text: For $\varepsilon>0$, choose $y=\iota_m(a)$ with $\|x-y\|<\varepsilon/(\|\omega\|+2)$, using density of the stages.
For $n\geq m$, the exact finite-stage compression identity gives $E_n(y)=0$.
This bound holds for every $n\geq m$, which is the required norm limit.

content.proof_summary: If $y=\iota_m(a)$ lies in a finite stage, rank-one compression gives $E_n(y)=0$ whenever $n\geq m$. For arbitrary $z\in A$, the projection norm bound and boundedness of $\omega$ give $\|E_n(z)\|\leq(1+\|\omega\|)\|z\|$, uniformly in $n$. Approximate the fixed $x$ by such a $y$, and apply this estimate to $x-y$.
